reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Scriver's OMMBID
clinicalPearls: Caused by deficiency of alpha-L-fucosidase, leading to accumulation of fucose-containing oligosaccharides, glycolipids, and glycoproteins
Presents along a spectrum, from a severe rapidly progressive infantile form to a milder, slowly progressive form with longer survival
Progressive neurological decline, coarse facies, dysostosis multiplex, and growth failure are core features
Angiokeratoma corporis diffusum, similar to that of Fabry disease, is characteristic, particularly in longer-surviving patients
Recurrent infections and dysautonomia with abnormal sweating can occur
Urinary oligosaccharide screening reveals fucosylated compounds rather than glycosaminoglycans
Diagnosis is confirmed by deficient alpha-L-fucosidase activity and FUCA1 gene testing
reference.pathophysiology: Fucosidosis is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in FUCA1, encoding the lysosomal enzyme alpha-L-fucosidase. This enzyme cleaves terminal fucose residues from fucose-containing glycoproteins, glycolipids, and oligosaccharides during their lysosomal degradation. Its deficiency causes accumulation of these fucosylated substrates in tissues throughout the body, including the nervous system, skin, and viscera, with excretion of fucosylated oligosaccharides in the urine. Storage in the central nervous system drives the progressive neurodegeneration, while systemic accumulation produces the coarse features, skeletal changes, and cutaneous angiokeratomas. Residual enzyme activity broadly correlates with the range from severe infantile to attenuated later-onset disease. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Other oligosaccharidoses such as alpha-mannosidosis and beta-mannosidosis
Mucopolysaccharidoses with coarse facies and dysostosis multiplex
Other causes of progressive neurodegeneration with organomegaly
additionalInvestigations: Leucocyte or fibroblast alpha-L-fucosidase enzyme assay
Urinary oligosaccharide analysis showing fucosylated compounds
Brain MRI for white matter and basal ganglia changes
Skin examination and biopsy for angiokeratomas
redFlags: Recurrent respiratory infections and failure to thrive
Cardiac involvement in more advanced disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the phenotype; severe infantile disease progresses rapidly with early mortality, while attenuated forms allow survival into later childhood or adulthood with progressive disability. Management is largely supportive, though haematopoietic stem cell transplantation has been attempted in selected cases.
pitfalls: Confusing the angiokeratomas with Fabry disease without appropriate enzyme testing
Screening only for glycosaminoglycans and missing the oligosaccharide pattern
Assuming a uniform severe course despite the wide clinical spectrum
Overlooking dysautonomia as part of the disorder
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
